title: Gaussian integration by parts on an explicit integrable domain
status: Authored admission source for an existing proof; not a retrospective pre-proof seal or independent acceptance

assumptions.text: E is a finite-dimensional real inner-product normed space with its Borel measurable structure. Completeness is derived.
f:E->R is Frechet differentiable at every point. The direction v is any vector of E.
f is absolutely Bochner integrable under gamma=stdGaussian(E).
x |-> <x,v> f(x) is absolutely Bochner integrable under that same gamma.
x |-> Df(x)[v] is absolutely Bochner integrable under that same gamma.

definitions.text: gamma is the actual centered identity-covariance Gaussian probability measure on E.
Df(x)[v] is the actual ambient real Frechet derivative of f at x applied to the fixed vector v. Differentiability ensures that the total derivative API does not supply an off-domain default.

For the proof, put d=dim_R E and omega(x)=(sqrt(2*pi)^(-1))^d exp(-||x||²/2). The existing Gaussian density theorem identifies gamma with omega times canonical Lebesgue measure. This density identity is derived, not an extra public input.

conclusion.text: integral_E <x,v> f(x) d gamma(x) = integral_E Df(x)[v] d gamma(x).
conclusion.quantifier_order: E and its structures; f and v; differentiability and the three Gaussian integrability hypotheses; exact scalar integral equality.

proof_topology.text: Apply the existing standard Gaussian density formula. Differentiate omega to obtain Domega(x)[v]=-omega(x)<x,v>.
Transfer the three Gaussian integrability assumptions to Lebesgue integrability of omega f, omega Df[v], and Domega[v] f. Positivity of omega justifies the density conversion.
Apply full-space scalar Frechet integration by parts, integral omega Df[v] = -integral Domega[v] f. Substitute the density derivative and transfer both integrals back to gamma.

boundaries: The direction can be zero; no unit-vector hypothesis is present.
All finite dimensions, including zero, are allowed. There is no positive-rank hypothesis.
No compact support, global Lipschitz bound, separate boundary decay or supplied Stein identity is assumed.
The theorem has an explicit analytic domain. It does not establish the three integrability conditions for an arbitrary observable.
When used by the Hermite product theorem, all three integrability conditions and differentiability are proved from polynomial Gaussian L2 membership; none becomes an extra Hermite hypothesis.
